openai.problem: Conflates self-consistency across repeated samples with adding a trained verifier to select the best candidate. Agreement-based selection and verifier-based ranking are separate controls.

openai.problem: The question makes purchasing across vendors essential, while the control describes different vendors as optional. It conflates using multiple distinct models with vendor diversification, and the aim attributes reliability gains specifically to vendor differences.

openai.problem: Bundles content cleaning, content reduction and context-window management. Correcting errors, summarizing a record and splitting unchanged text into chunks are independently selectable interventions.

openai.problem: Combines exact calculation with model-based prediction under 'deterministic computation.' The phrase 'final decisions' also implies clinical decision authority beyond producing scores or predictions.
openai.fix: Separate calculator/rule-based computation versus LLM calculation from prediction by a separate predictive model using LLM-extracted inputs versus direct LLM prediction. Replace 'final decisions' with the specific scores, measurements or predictions produced.

openai.problem: The comparator mixes unchanged image inputs with local model retraining. Those comparisons answer different questions: whether to preprocess images and whether to adapt inputs instead of adapting the model.
openai.fix: For the preprocessing decision, use images without the specified preprocessing as the comparator, holding the model and acquisition fixed. Do not treat local retraining as equivalent to raw/default images; retain it only as a distinct, explicitly supported adaptation comparison.

openai.problem: Bundles longitudinal information with spatial coverage. Adding prior exams is a different choice from supplying multiple views or slices of the current exam.
openai.fix: Split into prior/sequential examinations versus the current examination alone, and multiple current views or volumetric slices versus a single current/key image. Keep temporal change detection as an aim of the first comparison.

openai.problem: Bundles standards adoption with integration architecture. Point-to-point interfaces can use FHIR or DICOM, and an integrated data layer can use custom formats, so the stated alternatives are not opposites.
openai.fix: Separate standards-based exchange versus custom formats from an integrated AI data-ingestion layer versus siloed or point-to-point ingestion. Align each comparator with its own choice rather than presenting standards and integration as one inseparable package.

gemini.problem: Bundles two fundamentally different context-management strategies: summarizing/filtering (which discards data and relies on a model to compress information) and chunking (which preserves all data but requires iterative or retrieval-based processing architectures).
gemini.fix: Split into two distinct decisions: one focusing on summarizing or filtering long clinical text, and another focusing on chunking text to bypass context window limits.

gemini.problem: The wording goes beyond general member practices by naming highly specific clinical hardware and procedures (linked-color endoscopy, thin-section CT), which positions this as a narrow clinical workflow change rather than a general technical AI control.

final.question: Should model predictions decide which patients or time slots get limited outreach, review, follow-up intensity or staff time, rather than uniform allocation?

openai.problem: Patient-level targeting and demand-based staffing are separate decisions. Deciding which patients receive scarce services does not determine how many staff to schedule.
openai.fix: Split patient-level risk-targeted allocation, compared with universal, uniform or first-come allocation, from demand-forecast-based staffing, compared with historical-average staffing.

openai.problem: Reviewing only screen-positive records and confirming AI-generated scores are different workflows. Score confirmation need not reduce the number of records reviewed, but the control currently requires both selective review and score confirmation.
openai.fix: Separate LLM/NLP prescreening followed by human review of flagged or top-ranked records, compared with reviewing all records, from human confirmation of LLM-generated scores, compared with fully manual scoring.

openai.problem: This bundles system integration, automatic delivery, default-on adoption and co-design. An EHR-embedded tool can still be on-demand or opt-in.
openai.fix: Make the core question: 'Should AI output be embedded in existing clinical systems rather than provided through a standalone tool?' Remove automatic delivery, default-on use and co-design as requirements of embedding. Treat delivery and adoption defaults as distinct choices and co-design as an implementation practice.

openai.problem: Forming an independent judgment before seeing AI and retaining final decision authority are separate choices. AI-first presentation can still leave clinicians fully in charge, so the listed comparators do not isolate either choice.
openai.fix: Separate clinician-first versus AI-first assessment, holding clinician authority constant, from clinician-final versus AI-led decision-making. Treat clinician-only care as a separate comparison about adding AI, not as the comparator for presentation order or authority.

openai.problem: The question equates clinician supervision with preventing direct patient access. The control supports AI offered alongside clinician-led care, which can include patients interacting directly with a chatbot while receiving clinician support.
openai.fix: Ask: 'Should patient-facing AI be offered with clinician supervision and explanation rather than without clinician support?' Remove 'through ... rather than directly.' Use unsupervised AI as the comparator for supervision; distinguish clinician-only care as a comparison about adding AI.

openai.problem: Autonomous screening and AI participation in double reading involve different levels of autonomy and different care pathways. A backup reader also does not necessarily replace a human reader.
openai.fix: Split autonomous diabetic-retinopathy screening versus specialist referral from AI second/backup reading in breast screening versus standard two-radiologist double reading. Use 'replaces' only for configurations that actually remove a human reader.

openai.problem: Changing the order of work and assigning work to the appropriate staff are separate choices. Topic-based routing does not necessarily prioritize urgency.
openai.fix: Separate AI urgency-based worklist prioritization, compared with first-in-first-out order, from AI routing of messages, complaints and incident reports, compared with manual triage and assignment.

openai.problem: The review-before-use questions mix requiring review of AI output with adopting AI instead of human authoring. Patient-message replies also occur in both the release-review and drafting entries without a clear boundary between those decisions.
openai.fix: For the review entries, make reviewed versus unreviewed AI output the decision comparator; distinguish human-from-scratch production as an AI-adoption comparison. Keep llm_draft_documentation focused on AI drafts versus clinician-authored text, with clinician sign-off retained in both. Cross-reference patient-content release approval rather than treating drafting and approval as the same decision.

openai.problem: 'Every risk alert we deploy' turns examples of pairing predictions with response supports into an organization-wide requirement that the described practices do not establish.
openai.fix: Ask: 'Should a predictive alert be paired with a defined response protocol, nudge or documentation tool rather than delivered alone?' Keep the supported response supports as alternatives, without implying a mandate for every alert.

gemini.problem: Bundles the workflow decision to embed AI in the EHR with separate decisions about UI defaults ('default-on') and implementation processes ('co-design with users').
gemini.fix: Remove 'default-on use and co-design with users' to focus strictly on embedding AI outputs directly into existing workflow systems.

gemini.problem: Bundles fully autonomous point-of-care screening (replacing all humans) with using AI as a second reader (replacing one of two humans). These are distinct workflow choices with very different regulatory and safety profiles.
gemini.fix: Focus the control purely on replacing a human in a multi-reader workflow (e.g., 'Use AI as an independent second or backup reader') and remove the autonomous primary screening example.

gemini.problem: Duplicate coverage of patient message replies. Both controls dictate that clinicians must review and edit AI-drafted responses to patients before release.
gemini.fix: Remove 'patient message replies' from llm_draft_documentation to focus it exclusively on internal clinical documentation (e.g., discharge summaries, report impressions), leaving patient communication solely to review_patient_facing_content.

gemini.problem: Bundles operational workflow actions (response protocols, team rounding, documentation templates) with UI/UX design choices ('behavioral nudges').
gemini.fix: Remove 'behavioral nudges' to keep the focus strictly on linking risk predictions to defined clinical workflow and care pathways.

final.aim: Improve accuracy on complex clinical reasoning tasks

Higher vs lower reasoning effort setting

final.question: Should we fund iterative, expert-led prompt refinement and testing on pilot cases before go-live?
final.control: Refine prompts through repeated rounds of error analysis on pilot cases, clinician review, or automated optimization before deployment.
final.comparator: Single initial prompt used without refinement
final.aim: Reduce errors and improve agreement with clinicians before deployment

final.question: Should we split the task into a chain of smaller prompts instead of one large prompt?

final.question: Should we have the model review and revise its own answer before it is used?

final.comparator: Single-pass answer without self-review
final.aim: Catch and correct errors before outputs reach users

final.question: Should we add prompt instructions that guard against cognitive bias and clinically irrelevant demographic cues?
final.control: Instruct the model to ignore clinically irrelevant demographic or socioeconomic information, avoid stereotyping, and counter cognitive biases such as base-rate neglect.
final.comparator: Standard prompt without debiasing instructions
final.aim: Reduce biased or stereotyped outputs
variants: Ignore clinically irrelevant socioeconomic or demographic information

final.question: Should we instruct the model not to abandon a justified answer just because a user pushes back?
final.control: Instruct the model to avoid changing a justified answer solely because of user pressure, while still updating on new clinical information.
final.comparator: Standard prompt without anti-sycophancy instructions
final.aim: Reduce sycophantic capitulation to unfounded user pushback

Re-evaluate only when new evidence is given

final.question: Should we use zero or a validated low temperature rather than the default or a higher setting?
final.control: Set sampling temperature to zero or a validated low value for clinical tasks.
final.comparator: Default or higher temperature settings
final.aim: Improve reproducibility and consistency of clinical outputs

final.question: Where and when should instructions and key information go in the prompt or conversation?
final.control: Choose instruction placement, repetition and evidence timing deliberately: system role, periodic restatement, or staged evidence introduction, each assessed against its own baseline.
final.comparator: User-message placement, once-only instructions, or all evidence upfront, respectively
final.aim: Improve instruction adherence and reasoning across long or multi-turn interactions
variants: System role vs user message placement
Deferring diagnostic questions or salient evidence to later turns vs upfront

final.question: Should the system prompt restrict what the chatbot may advise and require history-taking before advice?
final.control: Set system instructions limiting chatbot scope and requiring history before advice, optionally with clinician-set goals and safety context.
final.comparator: Open-ended chatbot without scope or history-taking instructions
final.aim: Prevent unsafe or out-of-scope advice to patients
variants: History-taking before advice vs immediate advice
Clinician-set goals and safety context as part of tested package

final.question: Should we give the imaging model expert hints, reference atlases or visual markers alongside the image?

final.comparator: Image with plain prompt, or model self-generated intermediates where tested

final.question: Should we feed the speech recognition model a contextual prompt with local medical vocabulary?

final.comparator: Speech transcription without contextual vocabulary prompts

openai.problem: Bundles assigning the model a role or persona with adapting the answer for a particular reader. These are independently selectable prompt changes.
openai.fix: Separate role/persona assignment versus no assigned role from audience adaptation versus no audience specification. Keep tone, length and reading level under audience adaptation. Map only the member-supported comparisons to each.

openai.problem: Bundles requesting structured output with automatically validating it. Also, prompt instructions alone do not necessarily 'force' compliance with a schema.
openai.fix: Ask: 'Should we specify required fields, a template or allowed answers in the prompt?' Remove automatic validation from this prompt-only control and retain free-text output as the comparator.

openai.problem: Bundles a prompt-writing choice with enabling a model capability or changing its reasoning-effort setting. The comparator changes both prompt style and model mode.
openai.fix: Separate stepwise-reasoning prompts versus direct-answer prompts from native reasoning-mode or effort-setting comparisons. Use the actual mode or effort comparator reported by the relevant members rather than treating these as one prompting intervention.

openai.problem: Bundles debiasing with resistance to user pressure. The control also says to ignore 'sociodemographic information' without limiting that instruction to clinically irrelevant information, and 'hold position' can imply refusing justified corrections.
openai.fix: Separate debiasing instructions versus no debiasing instructions from anti-sycophancy instructions versus no anti-sycophancy instructions. Use 'ignore clinically irrelevant demographic information' and 'avoid changing a justified answer solely because of user pressure.'

openai.problem: Bundles sampling-temperature selection with fixing and archiving prompt templates. The question also specifies zero, while the control includes validated nonzero low values.
openai.fix: Ask: 'Should we use zero or a validated low temperature rather than the default or a higher setting?' Limit the control to temperature selection; remove fixed, archived prompt templates from this decision.

openai.problem: Combines three choices: instruction role placement, repetition during conversation, and timing of evidence introduction. The comparator changes all three together, so it does not identify which choice is being assessed.
openai.fix: Distinguish system-role versus user-message placement, repeated versus once-only instructions, and staged versus upfront evidence. Assign the supported member comparisons to each; if a member evaluates only the combined package, retain it as a package rather than implying separate effects.

openai.problem: Bundles restrictions on advice, history-taking prerequisites, and provision of clinician-set goals or safety context. The question additionally introduces handoff, which is not described in the control.
openai.fix: Remove 'handoff.' Separate scope restriction versus unrestricted scope from requiring history before advice versus no such requirement. Treat clinician-set goals and safety context according to the actual member intervention: as part of a tested package, or as a separate comparison only when supported.

openai.problem: Bundles replacing human abstraction with avoiding supervised-model training. Human abstractors and supervised models are different comparators, and 'zero-shot or structured-prompt' does not define one consistent intervention because structured prompts need not be zero-shot.
openai.fix: Separate the supported comparisons of LLM extraction versus expert human abstraction from zero-shot extraction versus supervised extraction models. Specify whether each LLM intervention is zero-shot, structured, or both. Frame the second comparison around the extraction approaches rather than broadly claiming to replace building annotated training sets.

openai.problem: Mixes supplying interpretive guidance with changing the image/input representation. It also combines two distinct comparators: no supplied guidance and model-generated intermediates. 'Chosen input representations' is too unspecified to define a reproducible choice.
openai.fix: Keep supplied expert hints, atlases or markers versus an image with a plain prompt as the guidance comparison. Distinguish supplied guidance versus model-generated intermediates where members evaluate that contrast. For representation-change practices, name the actual input variant and observed comparator separately rather than including them under generic 'visual hints.'

gemini.problem: Bundles assigning a persona to the model with tailoring the output to a specific audience or reading level. These are distinct prompting techniques.
gemini.fix: Split into two separate controls: 'persona_assignment' and 'audience_tailoring'.

gemini.problem: Bundles instructions for mitigating demographic bias with anti-sycophancy instructions (instructing the model not to agree with users under pressure). These address completely different failure modes.
gemini.fix: Split into 'debiasing_instructions' (for fairness) and 'anti_sycophancy_instructions' (for conversational robustness).

gemini.problem: This question compares an AI approach to manual human labor, which is a use-case validation or adoption decision, not a technical prompt configuration control.
gemini.fix: Remove this item from the prompting technical controls family, as it belongs in use-case evaluation or automation strategy.

gemini.problem: Bundles the architectural decision of where to place instructions (system role vs. user prompt) with the conversational strategy of when to restate them in long interactions.
gemini.fix: Split into 'system_prompt_placement' (system vs. user message) and 'periodic_instruction_restatement' (strategy for long context windows).

final.question: Should we require models to be trained with methods that correct for class imbalance so rare clinical outcomes are detected?
final.control: Apply imbalance-aware training, such as reweighted or focal losses, resampling, or balanced curation, and select models on rare-outcome sensitivity and calibration.
final.comparator: Otherwise comparable training without imbalance correction
final.aim: Improve detection of rare outcomes and limit overconfidence on majority classes
variants: Oversampling, undersampling, augmentation, or balanced curation
Post hoc threshold or calibration correction as alternative comparator

final.question: Should we require fairness-aware training methods that reduce performance gaps across patient demographic groups?
final.control: Apply fairness-aware training, such as fairness constraints, adversarial debiasing, or group-specific models, and select models on both accuracy and subgroup performance.
final.comparator: Otherwise comparable training without fairness-specific objectives
final.aim: Reduce subgroup performance gaps across sex, race, and other patient groups
variants: Group-specific models by sex or race with no-harm selection
Explicitly including or excluding sensitive attributes
Model selection on accuracy plus fairness metrics

final.question: Should we fine-tune or adapt a model to our own data, guidelines, and context instead of using an off-the-shelf model with prompting?
final.control: Fine-tune, continue pre-training, or otherwise adapt the model to institutional or device data, local guidelines, documentation formats, and culture.
final.comparator: Off-the-shelf model used as-is with zero- or few-shot prompting
final.aim: Improve task accuracy and fit to local practice, devices, and patient population
variants: Adapting content to local guidelines, formulary, and documentation standards

final.question: Should we require models trained on data from multiple sites and devices, including through federated learning?
final.control: Train or adapt models on multi-institution, multi-device data, pooled and harmonized or via federated or swarm learning when data cannot be shared.
final.comparator: Model trained on single-site or single-device data
final.aim: Improve generalizability across sites, scanners, and populations while protecting patient data
variants: Federated learning sharing model updates only
Federated vs centralized pooled training comparison

final.question: Should we host AI models within our own environment rather than sending patient data to an external vendor cloud API?
final.control: Host model inference on-premise, on-device, or embedded in scanner, PACS, or viewer infrastructure under health-system control, keeping patient data local.
final.comparator: Comparable-capability model accessed through an external vendor cloud API
final.aim: Protect patient data, control cost and latency, and increase institutional control over models
variants: Inference embedded in scanner, PACS, or viewer
Local inference server vs cloud-only inference

final.question: Should we keep updating deployed models, through scheduled retraining, clinician-correction loops, or targeted edits, rather than leaving them static?
final.control: Update deployed models at set intervals or from clinician-corrected errors, or apply targeted editing or steering, guarding against forgetting.
final.comparator: Static model trained once and never updated
final.aim: Maintain performance as data and practice drift and correct known errors or biases
variants: Scheduled retraining on recent local data
Expert review and correction loop feeding retraining
Test-time adaptation instead of full retraining

final.question: Should we train on supervision derived from reports, outcomes, routine data, or unlabeled data instead of full expert annotation?
final.control: Use weak, proxy, or objective outcome labels, or self-supervised pretraining on unlabeled data, instead of full manual expert labels, holding case selection constant.
final.comparator: Full manual expert annotation of the same cases
final.aim: Reduce annotation cost and label subjectivity while keeping model performance
variants: Workflow-derived or routine charted proxy labels
Report text or slide-level weak labels
Semi- or self-supervised pretraining on unlabeled data

final.question: Should we choose a specialized model variant, domain-specific or reasoning-enhanced, rather than a standard general-purpose model?
final.control: Select a domain-specific, task-specific, or reasoning-enhanced model variant matched to the clinical task and users, validated against the standard alternative.
final.comparator: Standard general-purpose model version used zero-shot
final.aim: Improve accuracy and reliability on specialized or complex clinical reasoning tasks
variants: General multimodal LLM zero-shot as alternative

final.question: Should we add synthetic or model-generated data to training when real labeled data are scarce or imbalanced?
final.control: Augment or pretrain with synthetic records, generated text, or simulated images, quality-filtered and mixed with real data.
final.comparator: Training on available real data only
final.aim: Improve performance and balance when real labeled data are scarce
variants: Quality filtering and real-synthetic mixing ratios

final.question: Should we lock the model's temperature and decoding settings low or deterministic for clinical use?
final.control: Set decoding temperature to zero or a tuned low value and fix inference settings per clinical task.
final.comparator: Default vendor temperature and sampling settings
final.aim: Reduce output variability and hallucination in clinical tasks
variants: Fixed top-p and other sampling parameters

final.question: Should we require safety alignment training on top of the base model?
final.control: Apply RLHF, preference optimization, or safety-constrained rewards targeting clinical safety rules.
final.comparator: Base or instruction-tuned model without safety-specific alignment
final.aim: Reduce unsafe, harmful, or rule-violating clinical outputs

final.question: Should we adopt deep learning image reconstruction to enable lower-dose or faster imaging protocols?
final.control: Use deep learning reconstruction, denoising, or synthesis to run lower-dose or shorter acquisition protocols.
final.comparator: Current standard-dose or standard-duration protocol with conventional reconstruction
final.aim: Reduce radiation dose and scan time while preserving diagnostic image quality
variants: Reconstruction-only comparison at matched acquisition settings

final.question: Should we pair the AI model with a rule-based or specialized-model layer rather than rely on one end-to-end model?
final.control: Combine rule-based NLP or specialized models with a general model in a staged or routed pipeline.
final.comparator: Single end-to-end general model
final.aim: Improve accuracy, reliability, and efficiency on defined subtasks

final.question: Should we invest in systematic curation and informed selection of training cases rather than using available or randomly chosen data?
final.control: Audit label consistency, handle label noise, deduplicate, enrich clinically important cases, and select cases for expert annotation by model uncertainty.
final.comparator: Available or randomly selected data with only basic cleaning, same labeling budget
final.aim: Improve accuracy and robustness per unit of annotation effort by reducing noise and redundancy
variants: Active learning by uncertainty or informativeness

final.question: Should we let clinicians build their own models with no-code AutoML platforms?
final.control: Provide code-free AutoML platforms so clinicians can label data and train task-specific models.
final.comparator: Data-scientist-led conventional development for the same clinical task
final.aim: Enable faster, lower-cost development of task-specific models by clinicians

openai.problem: Class-imbalance correction and subgroup-fairness training are separate choices. A model can use either without the other, and improved rare-outcome detection does not necessarily reduce subgroup performance gaps.
openai.fix: Split into imbalance-aware training versus otherwise comparable training without imbalance correction, and fairness-aware training versus otherwise comparable training without fairness-specific objectives. Assign rare-outcome detection and subgroup-gap reduction to their respective decisions.

openai.problem: This bundles deployment location, weight accessibility, and model size. Small or open-weight models can run in the cloud, and locally hosted models need not be small or open-weight.
openai.fix: Separate local/on-device versus cloud hosting, open-weight versus closed-weight model selection, and small versus large model selection. Keep the other attributes comparable within each contrast. Do not use large proprietary cloud models as the common comparator for all three choices.

openai.problem: The decision combines the source of supervision with the selection of cases for annotation. Active learning can still use full expert labels; it changes which cases are labeled, not the label source. Self-supervision is also not a label type.
openai.fix: Split into alternative label sources or supervision versus full expert labeling, with case selection held constant, and uncertainty-selected versus randomly selected cases for expert annotation at a comparable labeling budget. Replace the blanket phrase 'cheaper labels' with wording that distinguishes supervision source from annotation selection.

openai.problem: The comparator alternates between a reconstruction method and an acquisition protocol. Standard-dose acquisition can itself use deep learning reconstruction, so the comparison does not clearly distinguish algorithm replacement from dose or scan-time reduction.
openai.fix: For the stated question, define a protocol-level comparison: DL-enabled lower-dose or faster imaging versus the current standard-dose or standard-duration protocol using conventional reconstruction. Keep reconstruction-only comparisons at matched acquisition settings distinct from this protocol-level contrast.

openai.problem: The no-code comparator mixes a development-route comparison with a model-specialization comparison. Data-scientist-led development addresses who builds the model and how; comparison with general-purpose AI instead overlaps with domain_vs_general_model.
openai.fix: Make no_code_automl compare clinician-led no-code AutoML development with data-scientist-led conventional development for the same clinical task. Keep task-specific versus general-purpose model comparisons under domain_vs_general_model rather than using them to support claims about the no-code development route.

gemini.problem: Bundles model architecture and licensing (small, open-weight) with the deployment infrastructure (on-premise, embedded vs. cloud).
gemini.fix: Focus the decision specifically on local/private hosting (deploying models in a health system's own environment) versus using external proprietary cloud APIs.

gemini.problem: A Chief Health AI Officer would not recognize this as a general AI technical control; it is a highly specialized physics and equipment purchasing decision typically managed by radiology.
gemini.fix: Remove this item from the general AI model choice family, as it is a modality-specific hardware capability.

gemini.problem: Lacks a credible comparator. No AI leader strategically chooses 'uncurated available data'; data curation is a universal prerequisite, not a selectable alternative to doing nothing.
gemini.fix: Remove the decision, or reframe it as a choice between automated/AI-assisted curation methods versus manual expert data curation.

gemini.problem: Bundles addressing clinical class imbalance (e.g., detecting rare diseases) with demographic fairness (e.g., preventing racial bias), which involve different clinical, ethical, and regulatory strategies.
gemini.fix: Split into two distinct decisions: one focused on fairness-aware training to correct demographic bias, and another focused on handling clinical class imbalance for rare outcomes.

gemini.problem: Bundles weak/proxy labeling (using routine clinical data instead of expert labels) with active learning (using model uncertainty to select specific cases for human annotation).
gemini.fix: Focus this decision on the use of weak, proxy, or self-supervised labels versus full manual annotation, and optionally separate active learning into its own control.
